# Observation Report # Basic C Programming — 13 Laboratory Programs ## Objective of the Lab The objective of this laboratory exercise is to practice basic C programming concepts such as input and output, arithmetic and relational operators, conditional statements, the ternary operator, switch statements, loops, and basic data-type operations. The experiments are intended to develop problem-solving skills by applying these concepts to decision-making, calculations, data manipulation, and menu-based programs. ## Program 1: Even or Odd ## Problem Understanding The program accepts an integer as input and determines whether the number is even or odd. A number is even if it is completely divisible by 2; otherwise, it is odd. The program displays the corresponding result. ## Logic / Approach Used The input number is divided by 2 using the modulus operator. The remainder is checked using a condition. If the remainder is zero, the number is considered even. Otherwise, it is considered odd.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
nStores the input integer
remainderStores the remainder obtained when the number is divided by 2
## What I Observed I observed that the remainder obtained from n % 2 is zero for every even number, while an odd number produces a remainder of one. ## Program 2: Positive, Negative, or Zero ## Problem Understanding The program accepts an integer and determines whether its value is positive, negative, or exactly zero. The appropriate category is displayed as the output. ## Logic / Approach Used The input value is first compared with zero. If it is greater than zero, it is positive. If it is less than zero, it is negative. If neither condition is true, the value must be zero.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
nStores the input number
## What I Observed I observed that zero needs a separate condition because it is neither positive nor negative. --- ## Program 3: Character Checking ## Problem Understanding The program accepts a character as input and identifies whether it is an uppercase letter, lowercase letter, digit, or special character. The program displays the category to which the entered character belongs. ## Logic / Approach Used The character is compared with the ranges for uppercase letters, lowercase letters, and digits. The conditions are checked one by one. If the character does not belong to any of these ranges, it is treated as a special character.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
chStores the character entered by the user
## What I Observed I observed that the same character can be classified into only one of the specified categories based on its character range. Characters such as letters and digits are handled differently from symbols. ## Program 4: Leap Year ## Problem Understanding The program accepts a year and determines whether it is a leap year. The output indicates whether the given year contains an extra day in February. ## Logic / Approach Used The year is checked for divisibility by 400, or for divisibility by 4 while not being divisible by 100. If either condition is satisfied, the year is considered a leap year. Otherwise, it is not a leap year.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
yearStores the year entered by the user
## What I Observed I observed that simply checking whether a year is divisible by 4 is not sufficient because century years have a special condition. A century year is a leap year only when it is divisible by 400. ## Program 5: Memory Size of C Data Types ## Problem Understanding The program determines the amount of memory occupied by different C data types. It uses the sizeof operator to obtain the size of the specified data types and displays the results. ## Logic / Approach Used The sizeof operator is applied to different data types such as integer, character, floating-point, and double types. The returned size is displayed for each type. ## Important Variables and Their Purpose ---
VariablePurpose
sizeStores the memory size obtained for a data type
## What I Observed I observed that different data types can require different amounts of memory. The sizeof operator provides the size used by a data type in the current C environment. ## Program 6: Menu-Based Arithmetic Operations ## Problem Understanding The program accepts two numbers and a menu choice from the user. Based on the selected operation, it performs addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulus, or power and displays the calculated result. ## Logic / Approach Used First, the two input numbers and the user's menu choice are obtained. A switch statement is then used to select the required arithmetic operation. The selected operation is performed on the two values and the result is displayed. Division and modulus require appropriate handling because the second value cannot be zero.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
num1Stores the first input number
num2Stores the second input number
choiceStores the selected menu operation
resultStores the result of the selected operation
## What I Observed I observed that a switch statement makes the menu-based program easier to organize because each menu choice can be associated with a separate operation. I also noticed that division and modulus need special consideration when the second number is zero. ## Program 7: Swap Without a Temporary Variable ## Problem Understanding The program accepts two values and exchanges their contents without using an additional temporary variable. After the operation, the values of the two variables are displayed in swapped order. ## Logic / Approach Used The two variables are changed using arithmetic operations so that the value of each variable can be transferred to the other without creating a third variable. After the sequence of operations, the original values are exchanged.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
aStores the first value and participates in the swapping operations
bStores the second value and participates in the swapping operations
--- ## What I Observed I observed that two values can be exchanged without a temporary variable by using arithmetic operations. The intermediate values are important because each operation changes the information stored in the variables. ## Program 8: Swap Using a Temporary Variable ## Problem Understanding The program accepts two values and exchanges them using an additional temporary variable. The final output shows the two values after swapping. ## Logic / Approach Used First, the value of the first variable is stored in the temporary variable. The second value is then assigned to the first variable, and the saved value from the temporary variable is assigned to the second variable. This completes the exchange.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
aStores the first value
bStores the second value
tempTemporarily stores one value during the swap
## What I Observed I observed that using a temporary variable makes the swapping process easier to understand because the original value is safely stored before one variable is overwritten. ## Program 9: Perfect Square Without sqrt ## Problem Understanding The program accepts a number and determines whether it is a perfect square without directly using the square-root function. A number is identified as a perfect square if it can be expressed as the product of an integer by itself. ## Logic / Approach Used The program checks possible integer values starting from a suitable starting point. Each value is multiplied by itself and compared with the input number. If a multiplication result matches the input, the number is identified as a perfect square. If no matching value is found, it is not a perfect square.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
nStores the input number
iRepresents the possible integer whose square is being checked
foundIndicates whether a matching square has been found
## What I Observed I observed that a number is a perfect square when some integer multiplied by itself gives exactly the input value. The program can determine this without calculating the square root directly. --- ## Program 10: Student Grade Based on Marks ## Problem Understanding The program accepts a student's marks and determines the corresponding grade according to the specified mark ranges. The grade obtained from the appropriate range is displayed. ## Logic / Approach Used The marks are compared with the grade boundaries using an if-else structure. The conditions are checked in order until the range containing the entered marks is found. The corresponding grade is then displayed.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
marksStores the student's marks
gradeStores or represents the grade assigned based on the marks
## What I Observed I observed that the order of the conditions is important because each range must be checked correctly to assign the appropriate grade. Boundary values also affect which grade is selected. ## Program 11: Extended Menu Calculator with Error Handling ## Problem Understanding The program accepts two numbers and a menu choice to perform different arithmetic operations. It also handles invalid menu choices and prevents division by zero instead of performing an invalid calculation. ## Logic / Approach Used The program first accepts the numbers and operation choice. A switch statement selects the requested operation. Before division, the second number is checked to ensure that it is not zero. If an invalid menu option is entered, the program displays an appropriate error message instead of performing an operation.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
num1Stores the first input number
num2Stores the second input number
choiceStores the selected calculator operation
resultStores the calculated result
## What I Observed I observed that error handling is necessary in a calculator because not every input represents a valid operation. In particular, division by zero must be detected before performing the division, and invalid menu choices should be handled separately. ## Program 12: Largest of Three Using Ternary Operator ## Problem Understanding --- The program accepts three numbers and determines which one has the largest value. The largest number is displayed as the output. The comparison is performed using the ternary operator. ## Logic / Approach Used The first two numbers are compared and the larger value is selected. That value is then compared with the third number using another conditional expression. The final selected value represents the largest of the three inputs.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
aStores the first number
bStores the second number
cStores the third number
largestStores the largest value obtained from the comparisons
## What I Observed I observed that the ternary operator can perform a simple conditional selection in a compact form. By comparing intermediate results, the largest value among three numbers can be obtained. ## Program 13: Grade Point to Letter Grade ## Problem Understanding The program accepts a grade point or corresponding grade value and determines the appropriate letter grade according to the given grading scheme. The resulting letter grade is displayed. ## Logic / Approach Used The input grade point is passed to a switch statement. Each applicable case corresponds to a particular grade-point value and assigns or displays the associated letter grade. A default case can be used to handle an input that does not match the valid choices.
Important Variables and Their Purpose
VariablePurpose
gradePointStores the grade point entered by the user
gradeStores or represents the corresponding letter grade
## What I Observed I observed that a switch statement is useful when different fixed input values need to be mapped to specific outputs. The default case is also useful for handling values outside the expected grading options. ## Conclusion Through these experiments, I practiced different basic C programming techniques including conditional statements, the modulus operator, sizeof, switch, the ternary operator, arithmetic operations, and variable manipulation. I also understood the importance of checking input conditions and handling invalid cases such as division by zero. These programs helped me understand how individual C programming concepts can be combined to solve practical problems.
